summary: NISAR SAR Change Explorer is a local web app that finds and explains surface changes between two NISAR L2 GCOV radar acquisitions. A user loads an earlier (T0) and a later (T1) HH/HV scene and selects an area. The app returns a pixel-level change mask, measured backscatter statistics, and a plain-language AI interpretation that suggests what may have changed and how to verify it independently. Radar sees through clouds and darkness, but raw SAR is hard to read for non-specialists. Our tool turns NISAR change into something a researcher, emergency planner, or student can inspect and question, for example spotting possible flood expansion along a river corridor.
details:
What it does
NISAR SAR Change Explorer is a local web application that detects, measures and explains surface changes between two NISAR L2 GCOV radar acquisitions of the same area. It has three tabs:
- Pick: upload an earlier (T0) and a later (T1) HH/HV GCOV product and draw a region of interest on the radar preview.
- Change: an interactive before/after viewer with T0, T1 and Split views, a draggable comparison divider, zoom and pan, colour/greyscale display and full-screen mode.
- Results: the detector's change mask, a measured report and an AI-written interpretation. The report covers acquisition dates, area, median HH/HV backscatter, and signed T1−T0 differences for flagged vs. unflagged sectors.

How it works
1)Data preparation. The app reads the HHHH and HVHV power grids from both GCOV files and checks that they share the same projection and pixel spacing. It aligns them by an integer pixel shift only, so no resampling changes the measurements. Power is averaged to the detector's 20 m grid and converted to decibels.
2)Change detection. A shared ViT-H/14 encoder, adapted to NISAR data with masked-autoencoder pretraining, encodes both dates. A convolutional head fuses the mean and the absolute difference of the two feature maps, so the result does not depend on date order, and outputs a change score for every pixel. Large areas are processed as overlapping 224×224 tiles that are blended into one seamless change map.
3)Scene classification. A linear classifier uses features pooled around detected change regions and labels the scene as "water-related change" or "other change" when there are enough candidates.
4)Interpretation. Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct with a LoRA-fine-tuned decoder receives three aligned images (clean T0, clean T1 and a standalone detector mask) together with the measured statistics. It writes three short sections: what the radar shows, a possible explanation, and an independent way to check it. If the model is unavailable, a rule-based fallback reports only the measured radar patterns.

Benefits
Radar sees through clouds, smoke and darkness, which makes NISAR ideal for monitoring floods, shorelines, agriculture and land-surface change. Raw SAR imagery, however, is hard to interpret without specialist training. Our tool helps researchers, emergency planners and students quickly find where the radar signal changed and inspect it visually. The measurements always stay separate from the AI text, so every claim can be checked against the data.

Goals
We want to make NISAR change detection accessible to non-experts while staying scientifically honest. The app states its limits openly: detector flags are changes in radar backscatter, not confirmed causes, and weak radar returns alone do not prove water. Every interpretation comes with a suggestion for independent verification, such as optical imagery or another radar date.

Tools and technologies
- Machine learning: Python, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT (LoRA), safetensors.
- Data processing: h5py, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow.
-Application: a Python web server with an HTML/CSS/JavaScript front end (canvas-based zoom, pan and split view).
-Design and collaboration: Figma for the interface, GitHub for code, Hugging Face for model weights.

Current limitations
The detector was evaluated against automatically generated change targets, so its accuracy on independently reviewed scenes is not yet established. Classifier scores are not calibrated probabilities, and the AI interpretation can misstate the shape, direction or cause of a change. This is why the measured report and images are always shown next to it.
